stimulus.text:
Source 1. George Whitefield, 1751: 'As for the lawfulness of keeping slaves, I have no doubt, since I hear of some that were bought with Abraham's money, and some that were born in his house. — And I cannot help thinking, that some of those servants mentioned by the Apostles in their epistles, were or had been slaves. It is plain, that the Gibeonites were doomed to perpetual slavery, and though liberty is a sweet thing to such as are born free, yet to those who never knew the sweets of it, slavery perhaps may not be so irksome.'

Source 2. Germantown Quaker petition, 1688: 'These are the reasons why we are against the traffik of men-body.' The petition, written by German Quakers in Pennsylvania, was sent to the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, which set it aside without acting on it.
stimulus.source_note: Whitefield quoted verbatim from his 1751 letter, as reproduced in Princeton Review Ch 6 supplemental material; Germantown petition quoted verbatim (1688, public domain).

source: original; stimulus is an original secondary passage written for this question
stem: 'These are the reasons why we are against the traffik of men-body.' — Germantown Quaker petition, 1688. Which broader development best explains the context of this document?

options.text: The economic decline of the transatlantic slave trade in the late 1600s, which made slavery unprofitable.
options.misconception: The trade was expanding, not declining, in the late 1600s.

options.text: A ruling by an English court that slavery was illegal in the colonies.
options.misconception: No such ruling existed; slavery remained legal in the colonies.

options.text: The influence of Enlightenment philosophers on colonial assemblies.
options.misconception: The petition was a religious document, written before the Enlightenment reached colonial assemblies.

options.text: Quaker moral opposition to slavery, the earliest organized antislavery tradition in English America.

rationales.general:
1. Read what the petitioners say. They are against 'the traffik of men-body' — the buying and selling of people.
2. Ask who they are. German Quakers in Pennsylvania, writing from religious conviction.
3. Ask what their faith produced. Background: the earliest organized moral opposition to slavery in English America — even though the meeting set the petition aside.
4. Name the context. Quaker moral opposition, rooted in dissent, not in economics or philosophy.
Remember: when a document argues from conscience, ask which community's conscience it speaks for.
rationales.D: The petitioners were German Quakers in Pennsylvania, writing from religious conviction against 'the traffik of men-body.' Their faith produced the earliest organized moral opposition to slavery in English America — a protest that came from dissenters whose religion condemned the trade. Background: it came decades before the Enlightenment reached colonial assemblies. The other options are wrong: the trade was expanding, no court had ruled slavery illegal, and the petition was religious, not philosophical.
rationales.A: The trade was expanding, not declining, in the late 1600s.
rationales.B: No such ruling existed; slavery remained legal in the colonies.
rationales.C: The petition was a religious document, written before the Enlightenment reached colonial assemblies.
